# GitHub’s star-history API replaces identity-heavy pagination with weekly aggregates


By OpenTools Team


·


October 14, 2026


GitHub’s new repository star‑history endpoint returns weekly and daily aggregate counts, reducing large histories from thousands of identity‑bearing requests to a small trend dataset.


##


The endpoint returns trends without exposing every stargazer


GitHub’s new` GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/stargazers/history` endpoint returns aggregate star activity by week and day. It replaces the common pattern of paginating through every user who starred a repository and reconstructing a time series locally.


The response is ordered newest-first. Each week contains a total and daily counts beginning on Sunday. GitHub’s[REST documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/activity/starring) warns that week boundaries are not guaranteed to align with UTC, so consumers should preserve the returned dates rather than inventing a timezone conversion.


The dataset reveals interest over time while avoiding an identity list in the trend response.


##


One call can return 30 weeks, with a 100-page ceiling


The endpoint supports up to 30 weeks per request and a maximum page number of 100. Public repositories can be read without authentication. Fine-grained tokens need Metadata read access.


GitHub’s engineering account says a React-scale example fell from 2,511 requests to about 24. The exact savings depend on history length and page size, but the interface changes the unit of retrieval from individual users to time buckets.


That makes dashboards faster and reduces rate-limit pressure. It does not create unlimited history: clients still need pagination and must handle the documented page ceiling.


##


GitHub moved the expensive grouping into an indexed date-range query


GitHub says its first aggregate implementation still scanned millions of rows before grouping them. The production design instead performs indexed date-range counts for the requested weeks, avoiding a full identity-heavy history read for each request.


Exceptionally dense weeks remain a scaling edge case, according to the engineering post. Consumers should retain ordinary retry and backoff behavior rather than assuming every repository will respond with identical latency.


The architectural lesson is narrow: an aggregate endpoint can match the reader job better than exporting detailed records and discarding identities afterward.


##


Star history is an interest signal, not a conversion metric


GitHub describes stars as an approximate level of repository interest. A rising count can coincide with a release, conference talk or social post, but the API does not attribute the cause and does not report installs, active usage, retention or revenue.


Removed stars and historical corrections can affect totals. Use the returned values as GitHub’s current aggregate record, and label any before-and-after analysis with its time basis.


For product decisions, combine the series with repository traffic, package downloads or other qualified outcomes. Do not turn a visible line into a claim about adoption without supporting evidence.


##


Migration should preserve dates and delete unnecessary identity data


Replace stargazer pagination only where the job is trend analysis. Cache the aggregate response within an appropriate freshness window, preserve the returned date labels and validate a bounded interval against the previous series before removing old code.


If a pipeline collected user identities solely to draw a chart, stop retaining them after the aggregate migration. Keep identity-bearing access only for a separately justified reader job and permission boundary.


Follow[GitHub’s OpenTools organization page](https://opentools.ai/organizations/github) for material API changes.
